messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [rstan] thinning a fit object
parts:
[moved from issue to stan-users]

My question below.

> On Aug 13, 2015, at 3:36 PM, bgoodri <notifi...@github.com> wrote:
>
> Jonah had a solution
>
> sub_sample <- function(stanfit, n, keep_warmup = TRUE) {
> sim <- stanfit@sim
> samp <- sim$samples
> W <- sim$warmup
> I <- sim$iter
> sel <- c(if (keep_warmup) 1:W, sample((W + 1):I, size = n))
> subsamp <- lapply(samp, function(chain_samp) {
> lapply(chain_samp, function(x) x[sel])
> })
> stanfit@sim$samples <- subsamp
> stanfit
> }
>
> but I don't think we want to encourage thinning by actually implementing it in rstan.

Are you going to remove thinning support in calls to stan() or
sampling()? Or is it just that there's no reason to throw away
draws once you have them in memory? Also, is there a way to
stream output without saving it into memory?

What I'm imagining is that someone wants to plot 100 posterior
draws or something from a longer chain by writing a generic function
that plots all the draws in a fit object. I know how to thing
a specific parameter, like extract(fit)$theta[1:100, ...], but I
don't know how to do it for the whole fit object.

So the question is how should someone write functions to deal
with this kind of thing? I tend to just write very specialized
one-offs, but I figured there must be a more general approach.
Should I be using the sim slot of the stanfit object?

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [rstan] thinning a fit object
parts:
On Thursday, August 13, 2015 at 3:49:21 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Are you going to remove thinning support in calls to stan() or
sampling()?  Or is it just that there's no reason to throw away
draws once you have them in memory?
Also, is there a way to stream output without saving it into memory?

Not really, but I think a better alternative to this "I only want to do too few posterior predictive simulations" position is to define the thing in generated quantities, not store it, and look at its entries in get_posterior_means(). We should also probably implement a get_posterior_variances() in rstan. Maybe there are some cases where you want to throw away most of the draws with Jonah's function, but not for anything that you want to make important inferences about.

Ben
